title_en: Notice of the Supreme People's Court on Issuing the 32nd Batch of Guiding Cases
ruling_gist_en: 1. Where qualified subjects of labor relations enter into an agreement under the guise of "cooperative operation" or the like, but the rights and obligations specified in the agreement and the actual performance thereof meet the standards for determining the existence of a labor relation, and the worker claims that a labor relation exists with the employer, the people's court shall support such claim. 2. Where a written agreement executed between the employer and the worker contains terms on work content, remuneration, term of the labor contract, etc., that comply with the provisions of Article 17 of the Labor Contract Law, and the worker claims payment of double wages on the ground that the employer failed to conclude a written labor contract, the people's court shall not support such claim.
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Notice on Publishing the 32nd Batch of Guiding Cases

Fa [2022] No. 167

To: Higher People's Courts of all provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities directly under the Central Government; the Military Court of the People's Liberation Army; the Production and Construction Corps Branch of the Higher People's Court of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region:

Upon deliberation and decision by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, the following seven cases (Guiding Cases No. 179-185), including the case of Nie Meilan v. Beijing Lin's Brothers Culture Co., Ltd. regarding confirmation of labor relationship, are hereby published as the 32nd batch of guiding cases for reference in adjudicating similar cases.

July 4, 2022

Guiding Case No. 179

Nie Meilan v. Beijing Lin's Brothers Culture Co., Ltd. — Dispute over confirmation of labor relationship

(Deliberated and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, published on July 4, 2022)

Keywords: Civil/Confirmation of labor relationship/Cooperative operation/Written labor contract

Ruling Gist

1. Where parties qualified for a labor relationship enter into an agreement under the name of "cooperative operation" or the like, but the rights and obligations of both parties as agreed in the agreement and the actual performance thereof meet the criteria for determining a labor relationship, and a worker claims the existence of a labor relationship with the employer, the people's court shall support such claim.

2. Where a written agreement concluded between an employer and a worker contains clauses on work content, labor remuneration, term of the labor contract, etc., that comply with Article 17 of the Labor Contract Law, and the worker requests payment of double wages on the ground that the employer has failed to conclude a written labor contract, the people's court shall not support such request.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Articles 10, 17, and 82 of the Labor Contract Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

On April 8, 2016, Nie Meilan and Beijing Lin's Brothers Culture Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Lin's Brothers Company) entered into an "Agreement on Cooperative Establishment of a Tea Business Project," which provided as follows: "Article 1: Both parties agree that Party A shall make capital investment in the tea project and appoint Party B as the project manager for the tea business, with Party B responsible for the management and operation of the company. Article 2: After the project is launched, the parties shall jointly establish a company as circumstances permit, and Party B may be entitled to management shares. Article 3: Distribution of benefits: Prior to the establishment of the company, Party B shall be compensated on a basis of basic salary plus performance. After the establishment of the company, distribution shall be made in accordance with the shareholding proportion of both parties. Party B shall be responsible for management and operation, and the method of compensation shall be: basic salary + performance, bonus + share dividends. Article 4: Matters not covered during the operation of both parties shall be resolved through friendly negotiation. Article 5: This contract is executed in duplicate, one copy to be held by each shareholder of the company."

After the agreement was signed, Nie Meilan started working on the project, with her work content being responsible for the operation and management of the "Chinese Painting and Calligraphy" Art Tea House, primarily engaged in reception, tea sales, and other tasks. Lin Detang, the legal representative of Lin's Brothers Company, transferred a monthly basic salary of RMB 10,000 to Nie Meilan via bank transfer on the 15th of each month for the previous calendar month. Nie Meilan was required to obtain Lin Detang's approval for leave, and the actual number of attendance days affected the actual amount of salary paid. On May 6, 2017, Lin's Brothers Company notified Nie Meilan to terminate the cooperation agreement. Nie Meilan actually worked until May 8, 2017.

Nie Meilan applied for labor arbitration, claiming that the relationship between the parties was a labor relationship and requesting that Lin's Brothers Company pay her the double wage difference for failing to sign a written labor contract. Lin's Brothers Company contended that the relationship was one of cooperation. The Beijing Haidian District Labor and Personnel Dispute Arbitration Commission issued a ruling, Jing Hai Lao Ren Zhong Zi (2017) No. 9691, rejecting all of Nie Meilan's arbitration requests. Disagreeing with the arbitration ruling, Nie Meilan filed a lawsuit with the Beijing Haidian District People's Court within the statutory time limit.

Judgment

The Beijing Haidian District People's Court rendered a civil judgment on April 17, 2018, (2017) Jing 0108 Min Chu No. 45496: 1. Confirmed that a labor relationship existed between Lin's Brothers Company and Nie Meilan from April 8, 2016, to May 8, 2017; 2. Lin's Brothers Company was ordered to pay Nie Meilan RMB 22,758.62 as wages for the period from March 1, 2017, to May 8, 2017, within seven days after the judgment became effective; 3. Lin's Brothers Company was ordered to pay Nie Meilan RMB 103,144.9 as the double wage difference for the period from May 8, 2016, to April 7, 2017, for failing to sign a labor contract, within seven days after the judgment became effective; 4. Lin's Brothers Company was ordered to pay Nie Meilan RMB 27,711.51 as compensation for illegally terminating the labor relationship, within seven days after the judgment became effective; 5. Rejected Nie Meilan's other claims. Lin's Brothers Company appealed against the first-instance judgment. The Beijing First Intermediate People's Court rendered a civil judgment on September 26, 2018, (2018) Jing 01 Min Zhong No. 5911: 1. Affirmed items 1, 2, and 4 of the civil judgment (2017) Jing 0108 Min Chu No. 45496 of the Beijing Haidian District People's Court; 2. Reversed items 3 and 5 of the civil judgment (2017) Jing 0108 Min Chu No. 45496 of the Beijing Haidian District People's Court; 3. Rejected Nie Meilan's other claims. Lin's Brothers Company, dissatisfied with the appellate judgment, applied for retrial with the Beijing High People's Court. The Beijing High People's Court rendered a civil ruling on April 30, 2019, (2019) Jing Min Shen No. 986, rejecting Lin's Brothers Company's application for retrial.

Reasoning

The court in the effective judgment held: The "Agreement on Cooperative Establishment of a Tea Business Project" signed between the applicant, Lin's Brothers Company, and the respondent, Nie Meilan, was voluntarily signed, did not violate mandatory laws or regulations, and was a valid contract. In determining the nature of the contract, it should be based on the legal relationship involved in the contract content, i.e., the rights and obligations established by the parties to the contract. Article 1 of the agreement explicitly stipulated the appointment of Nie Meilan as the project manager for the tea business. The term "appointment" generally indicates an intention to hire a worker to provide labor. Article 3 of the agreement stipulated the method of compensation for Nie Meilan. Regardless of whether the target company contemplated by both parties was established before or after, Nie Meilan could receive remuneration such as "basic salary" and "performance," which clearly differs from the distribution of returns in a cooperative operation. The typical features of a cooperative operation contract are joint capital contribution and shared risks. In this case, the contract neither stipulated Nie Meilan's capital contribution ratio nor shared risks, which is inconsistent with a cooperative operation contract. Based on the relevant evidence in this case, Nie Meilan was subject to the management of Lin's Brothers Company, reported monthly on the attendance of employees, allocation of funds, expenditures, sales, work plans, and applications for petty cash, etc., and the amount of salary paid was closely related to the number of days attended. The relationship formed between the parties in the performance of the contract conformed to the dual characteristics of personal subordination and economic subordination in a labor relationship. Therefore, the original judgment finding that a labor relationship existed between the applicant and the respondent was not erroneous. The cooperation agreement signed by the parties could also be regarded as a written labor contract. Although it lacked some necessary clauses, this did not affect the validity and effect of the agreed clauses, and it could still serve to fix the labor relationship and rights and obligations between the parties. The second-instance court's judgment to revise the case accordingly was correct. On May 6, 2017, Lin's Brothers Company issued a "Notice of Termination of Cooperation Agreement" to Nie Meilan, informing her of the termination of the cooperation between the parties. This constituted an expression of intent to dissolve the labor relationship between the parties. According to Article 6 of the Several Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Civil Procedures, in a labor dispute case involving a decision made by the employer on dismissal, expulsion, removal, rescission of the labor contract, etc., the employer bears the burden of proof. Since Lin's Brothers Company failed to provide relevant evidence of the reason for dissolving the labor relationship, it should bear the adverse consequences. The second-instance court's judgment based on the specific circumstances and relevant evidence of this case was not erroneous.

(Judges of the effective judgment: Chen Weihong, Fu Zhongliang, Peng Hongyun)

Guiding Case No. 180

Sun Xianfeng v. Huaian West District Human Resources Development Co., Ltd. — Dispute over labor contract

(Deliberated and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, published on July 4, 2022)

Keywords: Civil/Labor contract/Rescission of labor contract/Assessment of legality

Ruling Gist

When a people's court assesses the legality of an employer's unilateral rescission of a labor contract, it shall take the content of the notice of rescission issued by the employer to the worker as the basis for determination. During the trial of a case, if the employer, beyond the basis and reason stated in the notice of rescission of the labor contract, separately raises that the worker had other serious violations of the employer's rules and regulations during the performance of the labor contract, and on that basis contends that the conditions for rescinding the labor contract are satisfied, the people's court shall not support such contention.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Article 39 of the Labor Contract Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

On July 1, 2016, Sun Xianfeng (Party B) and Huaian West District Human Resources Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as West District Company) (Party A) signed a labor contract, stipulating: the term of the labor contract was from July 1, 2016, to June 30, 2019; Party B's place of work was Lianyungang, engaged in mail collection and delivery and driver positions; if Party B seriously violated Party A's labor discipline or rules and regulations, Party A could immediately rescind this contract without bearing any economic compensation; if Party A rescinded or terminated the labor contract in breach of contract, it should pay Party B economic compensation or damages in accordance with the law and the provisions of this contract; various rules and regulations legally formulated and published by Party A, such as the Employee Handbook, Regulations on Rewards and Punishments, and Regulations on Employee Attendance Management, were attached to this contract as appendices and had the same effect as this contract. Subsequently, Sun Xianfeng, as arranged by West District Company, was responsible for the mail collection and delivery work of SF Express in the Duigougang Town area, Guannan County, Jiangsu Province. Starting from August 25, 2016, West District Company settled Sun Xianfeng's wages to his bank account monthly. As of September 25, 2017, Sun Xianfeng's average salary for the preceding 12 months was RMB 6,329.82. On September 12, October 3, and October 16, 2017, Sun Xianfeng successively committed disciplinary violations such as failing to wear work uniforms during working hours, swiping time cards for others, and leaving insulting messages against company supervisors on the company's public platform. Subsequently, West District Company, based on the Regulations on Rewards and Punishments, with the joint signature and confirmation of the responsible person of the employing department, the responsible person of the recommending department, the responsible person of the trade union, and the responsible person of the human resources department, imposed deductions of 2 points, 10 points, and 10 points respectively on Sun Xianfeng for the aforementioned disciplinary violations, but the specific time of the deduction of points was difficult to determine.

On October 17, 2017, Sun Xianfeng was suspended from work by the employing department of his unit on the grounds of failing to timely turn over business funds during his tenure. The next day, Sun Xianfeng went to the unit to clock in, but the information showed that the card swiping data could not be entered. On October 25, 2017, West District Company issued a certificate of resignation, stating that Sun Xianfeng had officially resigned from West District Company as of October 21, 2017, had completed the procedures, and no longer had any labor relationship with the company. On October 30, 2017, West District Company issued a notice of rescission of the labor contract, stating that Sun Xianfeng had been absent without leave for more than three consecutive days from October 20, 2017, without applying for leave or obtaining approval from any leader. Based on relevant national laws and regulations and the company's rules and regulations, the company decided to rescind the labor relationship with Sun Xianfeng as of October 20, 2017, requiring him to handle relevant procedures before November 15, 2017, and if he failed to do so, he would bear the consequences. Subsequently, Sun Xianfeng applied for labor arbitration to the Guannan County Labor and Personnel Dispute Arbitration Commission. After the arbitration award, Sun Xianfeng, dissatisfied, filed a lawsuit with the court, requesting West District Company to pay compensation for illegal rescission of the labor contract totaling RMB 68,500.

During the trial of the case, West District Company argued that Sun Xianfeng, during his tenure, had committed disciplinary violations such as failing to wear work uniforms as required, swiping time cards for others, insulting supervisors, and failing to timely turn over business funds in accordance with the company's rules and regulations, which constituted serious violations of the employer's rules and regulations; and that starting from October 20, 2017, Sun Xianfeng had been absent without leave for many days without applying for leave or obtaining approval, and the company rescinded the labor relationship with Sun Xianfeng as of October 20, 2017, in accordance with the law, which was lawful.

Judgment

The Guannan County People's Court of Jiangsu Province rendered a civil judgment on November 15, 2018, (2018) Su 0724 Min Chu No. 2732: 1. The defendant, West District Company, shall pay the plaintiff, Sun Xianfeng, economic compensation of RMB 18,989.46 within ten days after this judgment takes legal effect. 2. Reject the plaintiff Sun Xianfeng's other claims. West District Company appealed. The Lianyungang Intermediate People's Court of Jiangsu Province rendered a civil judgment on April 22, 2019, (2019) Su 07 Min Zhong No. 658, dismissing the appeal and affirming the original judgment.

Reasoning

The court in the effective judgment held: An employer's unilateral rescission of a labor contract is based on the worker's illegal, disciplinary, or breach-of-contract conduct, and the assessment of its legality should also be based on the facts, evidence, and relevant laws existing at the time of the decision to rescind the labor contract. The notice of rescission of the labor contract served by the employer to the worker is the employer's expression of intent to rescind the labor contract with the worker and is legally binding on the employer. The notice of rescission of the labor contract clearly states the basis and reason for the rescission. When a people's court hears a dispute over the rescission of a labor contract, it should examine the matter based on the facts, evidence, and laws at the time of the decision and should not exceed the content and scope stated in the notice of rescission of the labor contract. Otherwise, it would deviate from the review content of the legality of the rescission of the labor contract that is the subject of the dispute between the employer and the worker, leading to inconsistency between the court's ruling and the parties' claims and the focus of the dispute; at the same time, it would violate the fundamental principle of good faith that civil subjects should uphold when engaging in civil activities, resulting in an imbalance in the protection of the rights and interests of both employers and workers.

In this case, the labor contract signed between Sun Xianfeng and West District Company was the true expression of the parties' intentions and was legal and valid. The appendix to the labor contract, the Regulations on Rewards and Punishments, as the employer's management rules and regulations, did not violate the mandatory provisions of laws and administrative regulations, was legal and valid, and was binding on both parties. According to the Regulations on Rewards and Punishments, if an employee is absent without leave for three consecutive days (including three days) or more, the company has the right to impose a category 5 penalty, i.e., rescind the contract and never re-employ. The notice of rescission of the labor contract served by West District Company to Sun Xianfeng clearly stated that the reason for the rescission was that Sun Xianfeng had been absent without leave for more than three days. The content that Sun Xianfeng asked the court to review was also the legality of West District Company's decision to rescind the labor contract on the ground that Sun Xianfeng had been absent without leave for more than three days. Therefore, the court's review of the legality of West District Company's rescission of the labor contract should also be limited to the content stated in the notice of rescission of the labor contract and should not go beyond the scope of this dispute. Although West District Company also argued during the trial that Sun Xianfeng had other disciplinary violations during his employment, such as failing to timely turn over business funds, failing to wear work uniforms, swiping time cards for others, and leaving insulting messages against company supervisors on the company's public platform, which also constituted serious violations of the employer's rules and regulations and gave the company the right to rescind the labor contract, based on the evidence in the case and West District Company's statements, West District Company, knowing of the existence of the above conduct, did not propose to rescind the labor contract but actively proposed to reassign Sun Xianfeng to other work. When issuing the notice of rescission of the labor contract to Sun Xianfeng, it did not cite the above conduct as a reason for rescission. The court did not support the above argument raised by West District Company during the litigation.

West District Company rescinded the labor contract on the ground that Sun Xianfeng had been absent without leave for more than three days, and therefore bore the burden of proof to prove the fact that Sun Xianfeng had been absent without leave for more than three days. However, West District Company only provided its own employee attendance sheet, which was not signed or confirmed by Sun Xianfeng. Sun Xianfeng did not acknowledge it and argued that he was suspended from work by the company's leaders and provided a video showing the failure to swipe the card. Since Sun Xianfeng was suspended from work during his employment, West District Company failed to provide evidence to prove whether it notified Sun Xianfeng to report to the company later, how it notified him, and when it notified him. Thus, the fact that Sun Xianfeng was absent without leave for more than three days was unclear, and West District Company should bear the adverse consequences of failing to prove it. Its rescission of the labor contract on the ground that Sun Xianfeng was absent without leave in violation of the company's rules and regulations lacked factual basis and constituted an illegal rescission of the labor contract.

(Judges of the effective judgment: Wang Xiaojiao, Li Ji, Dai Liguo)

Guiding Case No. 181

Zheng v. Honeywell Automation Control (China) Co., Ltd. — Dispute over labor contract

(Deliberated and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, published on July 4, 2022)

Keywords: Civil/Labor contract/Rescission of labor contract/Sexual harassment/Rules and regulations

Ruling Gist

Where a management personnel of an employer receives a complaint from an employee who has been sexually harassed, the management personnel shall take reasonable measures to deal with it. If the management personnel fails to take reasonable measures or engages in conduct such as condoning the sexual harassment or interfering with the investigation of the sexual harassment, and the employer rescinds the labor contract on the ground that the management personnel failed to fulfill their job duties, thereby seriously violating the rules and regulations, and the management personnel claims that the rescission of the labor contract is illegal, the people's court shall not support such claim.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Article 39 of the Labor Contract Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

Zheng joined Honeywell Automation Control (China) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Honeywell Company) in July 2012, serving as a channel sales manager. Honeywell Company had established a training mechanism for preventing workplace sexual harassment, and Zheng had received relevant training. Honeywell Company's Code of Business Conduct provided that managers and supervisors "should ensure that subordinates can speak freely without fear of retaliation, and that all concerns or issues are resolved professionally and in a timely manner," and did not allow any retaliatory conduct. The 2017 version of the Employee Handbook provided that engaging in sexual harassment against others, violating the company's Code of Business Conduct, and making false statements during internal company investigations were disciplinary violations that would lead to immediate dismissal. The above rules and regulations were discussed at a communication meeting of the company's trade union before implementation.

The labor contract between Zheng and Honeywell Company stipulated that Zheng confirmed and agreed that the company's existing Employee Handbook and Code of Business Conduct and other rules and regulations formed part of this contract. After the Employee Handbook was revised, Zheng again signed a letter of confirmation, stating that he had read, understood, and accepted the contents of the 2017 version of the Employee Handbook and was willing to abide by the company's policies as a precondition for working at Honeywell Company.

On August 30, 2018, Zheng, believing that the relationship between his subordinate female employee Ren and his superior Deng (married) was somewhat strained, spoke with Ren to "ease" the relationship between the two. Zheng mentioned that he had observed the previous day that Deng said something to Ren, and Ren did not respond, and that he had specifically gone to Ren to help smooth things over. Ren mentioned that when she first joined the company, she had shown Zheng screenshots of WeChat messages containing sexual harassment sent by her indirect superior Deng. Zheng responded at that time, "I just don't want to get involved in this," "I don't want to answer you about this going forward," and "I think it's a bit strange, but I dare not ask." During the conversation, Ren emphasized that Deng was sexually harassing her, that Deng demanded a romantic relationship with her, and that he continued to harass her after she refused. Zheng should not blame her for not responding to Deng, nor should he come on Deng's behalf to reprimand her. Zheng then said, "If you work like this, it makes me very sad," "The more you hold yourself aloof, the more he thinks he can do something to you," and "He is so direct; if it were me, I would get close to you first, feel you out, and then chat."

Later, in November 2018, citing Ren's lack of sociability as a reason, Zheng proposed to the Human Resources Department of Honeywell Company that Ren's labor contract be terminated, but failed to provide a reasonable basis for such termination. The Human Resources Department subsequently approached Ren to understand the situation. Ren informed the HR Department that she was being harassed by her indirect superior Deng, that Zheng had intentionally or unintentionally facilitated her relationship with Deng, and that she was being retaliated against for refusing the harassment. Honeywell Company then launched an investigation.

On January 15, 2019, Honeywell Company conducted an investigation of Zheng and prepared an investigation record. Zheng did not sign the investigation record but made many modifications to the answers recorded in the record regarding the company's inquiries. Regarding the question recorded in the investigation record as to whether any female employee had reported to Zheng that Deng had said inappropriate things to her or had sexually harassed her, the recorded answer was "no," and Zheng did not modify this.

On January 31, 2019, Honeywell Company issued a "Unilateral Termination Letter," citing that Zheng failed to fulfill his managerial duties, took no measures to help his subordinate stop suffering from harassment after she reported harassment by her indirect superior, instead retaliated against her, and made false statements regarding the above facts during the investigation. On this basis, Honeywell Company terminated the labor contract with Zheng.

On July 22, 2019, Zheng applied for arbitration to the Shanghai Labor Dispute Arbitration Committee, requesting Honeywell Company to pay compensation of RMB 368,130 for wrongful termination of the labor contract. This request was not supported by the arbitration award. Dissatisfied, Zheng filed a lawsuit with the same request in the Shanghai Pudong New Area People's Court.

Judgment

The Shanghai Pudong New Area People's Court rendered a civil judgment ( [2020] Hu 0115 Min Chu No. 10454) on November 30, 2020, dismissing Zheng's claims. Dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, Zheng filed an appeal. The Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court rendered a civil judgment ( [2021] Hu 01 Min Zhong No. 2032) on April 22, 2021, dismissing the appeal and affirming the original judgment.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held that the issues in dispute in this case were: First, whether the "Employee Handbook" and the "Code of Business Conduct," which Honeywell Company relied upon to terminate Zheng's labor contract, were binding on Zheng; Second, whether Zheng had committed serious disciplinary violations sufficient to justify the termination of the labor contract.

With regard to the first issue: whether the "Employee Handbook" and the "Code of Business Conduct," which Honeywell Company relied upon to terminate Zheng's labor contract, were binding on Zheng. The evidence on record showed that the 2017 version of the "Employee Handbook" and the "Code of Business Conduct," to which Zheng objected, were discussed at Honeywell Company's union communication meetings in September 2017 and December 2014, respectively. The labor contract signed between Zheng and Honeywell Company expressly stipulated that the "Employee Handbook" and the "Code of Business Conduct" were integral parts of the labor contract, and that Zheng had read, understood, and accepted these policies. After the revision of the "Employee Handbook," Zheng also signed a confirmation form again, confirming that he had read, understood, and was willing to accept the 2017 version of the "Employee Handbook" and would abide by company policies as a prerequisite for working at Honeywell Company. Under these circumstances, the "Employee Handbook" and the "Code of Business Conduct" of Honeywell Company should be binding on Zheng.

With regard to the second issue: whether Zheng had committed serious disciplinary violations sufficient to justify the termination of the labor contract. First, the evidence on record showed that Honeywell Company had established a workplace sexual harassment prevention training mechanism, and Zheng had also received relevant training. Honeywell Company's "Code of Business Conduct" required managers, supervisors, and other management personnel to professionally and promptly help resolve concerns or issues raised by subordinates, and not to retaliate. Honeywell Company's 2017 version of the "Employee Handbook" also listed violations of the Company's "Code of Business Conduct" as serious disciplinary offenses that would lead to immediate dismissal. Now, although Zheng claimed that the female employee in question had not provided tangible evidence of being harassed, and that he could not determine the truth or falsity of the harassment, it is evident from Zheng's comments in the recorded conversation on August 30, 2018, regarding the WeChat screenshots shown to him by the female employee when she first joined the company—"I think it's a bit strange, but I dare not ask" and "I just don't want to get involved in this"—that Zheng himself did not consider the WeChat content to be normal communication between colleagues. Moreover, when the female employee repeatedly emphasized that her indirect superior had been harassing her, Zheng did not actively respond to help resolve the issue. Instead, he said, "He is so direct; if it were me, I would get close to you first, feel you out, and then chat." His actions were aimed at actively facilitating an improper relationship between his subordinate and his superior. Zheng's conduct clearly violated his duties as a department head of Honeywell Company, and his answers were also contrary to public order and good customs. Furthermore, according to Zheng's own statements, he should have clearly understood the reason for the poor relationship between the female employee and her indirect superior after the conversation on August 30, 2018. However, Zheng not only failed to take proactive measures but instead considered the female employee's handling of the matter inappropriate. After Ren explicitly expressed her resistance to Deng's sexual harassment, Zheng proposed to the HR manager in mid-November 2018 that Ren had an unsociable personality and hoped the company would terminate Ren's labor contract. Based on this, Honeywell Company's claim that Zheng retaliated against the female employee was also a reasonable inference. Second, the 2017 version of Honeywell Company's "Employee Handbook" expressly provided that making false statements during an internal company investigation constituted a serious disciplinary offense that would lead to immediate dismissal. The investigation record from January 15, 2019, provided by Honeywell Company, showed that Zheng had made false statements during the investigation. Although Zheng claimed that the investigation record did not accurately record what he said and that he was not allowed to make many modifications, this assertion contradicted the fact that Zheng had made many modifications to the answers recorded in the investigation record. The court did not accept this claim. The investigation record could serve as a basis for determining that Zheng had made false statements.

In summary, the various grounds for appeal raised by Zheng could hardly support his claim on appeal. Honeywell Company's assertion that Zheng had committed serious disciplinary violations was well-founded and did not constitute wrongful termination of the labor contract. Zheng's appeal request for Honeywell Company to pay compensation of RMB 368,130 for wrongful termination of the labor contract was not supported.

(Judges of the effective judgment: Sun Shaojun, Han Donghong, Xu Yan)

Guiding Case No. 182

Peng Yuxiang v. Nanjing Urban Construction and Development (Group) Co., Ltd. — dispute over claim for labor remuneration

(Discussed and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on July 4, 2022)

Keywords: civil, claim for labor remuneration, bonus, approval obligation

Ruling Gist

If an employer stipulates that a worker may receive a bonus upon achieving certain performance targets, and the employer refuses without justifiable reason to fulfill its approval obligation, and a worker who meets the bonus conditions claims that the conditions for receiving the bonus have been satisfied and that the employer should pay the bonus in accordance with the regulations, the people's court shall support the claim.

【Related Laws】

Article 4 of the Labor Law of the PRC, Article 3 of the Labor Contract Law of the PRC

【Basic Facts】

Nanjing Urban Construction and Development (Group) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Chengkai Company) formulated the "Interim Measures for Rewarding the Introduction of Investment Projects of Nanjing Chengkai Group" (hereinafter referred to as the "Reward Measures") in August 2016. The Measures stipulated that for successful introduction of commercial housing projects, Chengkai Company would comprehensively consider factors such as project scale, annualized average profit margin, and consolidated statement, and determine the total reward amount based on the approved expected profit or income of the project, at a rate of 0.1% to 0.5%. The reward was to be applied for by the Investment and Development Department after determining the specific reward composition for the department or other personnel, and then to be distributed after review and approval by the company's leadership. In February 2017, Peng Yuxiang joined Chengkai Company as Manager of the Investment and Development Department. In June 2017, the Investment and Development Department formed a "Meeting Minutes," confirming that the internal reward distribution plan was that the department manager would receive 75% of the department's bonus, and the other project participants would receive 25% of the department's bonus.

During Peng Yuxiang's tenure, the Investment and Development Department he led successfully introduced six projects: Wuxi Hongmei Xintiandi, Yangzhou GZ051 plot, Rugao York Town, Xuzhou Jiaozhuang, Gaoyou Hongji Wanhecheng, and Xuzhou Pengcheng Machinery. Subsequently, for these six projects, the Investment and Development Department submitted six reward applications to Chengkai Company.

Up to the time Peng Yuxiang left Chengkai Company, Chengkai Company had not paid the above rewards. After going through labor arbitration procedures, Peng Yuxiang filed a lawsuit with the court within the statutory time limit, requesting Chengkai Company to pay rewards of RMB 1,689,083.

During the trial of the case, Chengkai Company acknowledged that the six projects in question preliminarily met the reward conditions stipulated in the "Reward Measures." However, it argued that Peng Yuxiang's request for payment of rewards could not be established on the grounds that although the total reward amounts for the three projects including Wuxi had been approved, the specific details of the bonus distribution had not been approved, and that the reward applications for the three projects including Xuzhou had not been approved. When the court asked, "If Peng Yuxiang now submits further reward applications for the above projects, will Chengkai Company initiate the review process?", Chengkai Company expressly refused and stated that it would not initiate the approval process for the six projects in the future. In addition, Chengkai Company also claimed that Peng Yuxiang had committed serious dereliction of duty in the Wuxi Hongmei Xintiandi project and the Rugao York Town project, that these two projects had suffered serious losses, and that Chengkai Company had already paid Peng Yuxiang a reward for outstanding land acquisition performance, but it did not submit sufficient evidence to prove these claims.

【Judgment】

The Nanjing Qinhuai District People's Court rendered a civil judgment ( [2018] Su 0104 Min Chu No. 6032) on September 11, 2018, dismissing Peng Yuxiang's claims. Dissatisfied, Peng Yuxiang filed an appeal. The Nanjing Intermediate People's Court of Jiangsu Province rendered a civil judgment ( [2018] Su 01 Min Zhong No. 10066) on January 3, 2020: 1. Setting aside the civil judgment ( [2018] Su 0104 Min Chu No. 6032) of the Nanjing Qinhuai District People's Court; 2. Chengkai Company shall pay Peng Yuxiang a reward of RMB 1,259,564.4 within fifteen days from the effective date of this judgment.

【Reasoning】

The effective judgment of the court held: The issue in dispute in this case was whether Chengkai Company should, in accordance with the "Reward Measures," distribute rewards to the Investment and Development Department where Peng Yuxiang worked for the six projects including Wuxi Hongmei Xintiandi.

First, from the perspective of the reward targets set by the "Reward Measures," the Investment and Development Department's primary responsibility was to introduce projects, and it played a leading role in introducing various projects for Chengkai Company. Therefore, it was an eligible recipient of the reward under the Measures. From the perspective of the reward conditions set by the "Reward Measures," the Investment and Development Department had successfully introduced for Chengkai Company the six projects, including Wuxi Hongmei Xintiandi, Yangzhou GZ051 plot, Rugao York Town, Xuzhou Jiaozhuang, Gaoyou Hongji Wanhecheng, and Xuzhou Pengcheng Machinery, which were in line with Chengkai Company's strategic development goals. Thus, these projects met the reward conditions stipulated in the Measures. Accordingly, for the six projects in question, the Investment and Development Department where Peng Yuxiang worked had formally satisfied the conditions for claiming the reward as prescribed by the employer. If Chengkai Company disagreed with distributing the corresponding reward, it should explain the reasons and provide evidence to that effect. However, in this case, Chengkai Company could not prove that the Wuxi Hongmei Xintiandi project and the Rugao York Town project suffered losses, nor could it prove that Peng Yuxiang had indeed committed dereliction of duty in those two projects. Its claim that Peng Yuxiang should not receive a duplicate reward also lacked a corresponding basis and could not be established. Therefore, the court did not accept Chengkai Company's argument that the Investment and Development Department where Peng Yuxiang worked did not substantially meet the conditions for receiving the reward under the "Reward Measures."

Second, the fact that the reward applications for the six projects in question had not been reviewed or that the approval process had not been completed could not constitute a reason for Chengkai Company to refuse to pay Peng Yuxiang the project bonus. As the establisher of the bonus, Chengkai Company had the right to set corresponding assessment standards, assessment, or approval procedures. Among these, the assessment standards were substantive evaluation factors determining whether an employee could receive the bonus, while the assessment procedures were procedural steps set by Chengkai Company to exercise its assessment authority. Unless otherwise specifically provided, since the procedures themselves did not involve the criteria for evaluating the bonus, whether or not the approval process had been completed could not become a substantive evaluation element for whether an employee could receive the bonus. Chengkai Company could not attempt to obstruct the realization of Peng Yuxiang's substantive right to receive the bonus on the grounds that the approval process for the six projects had not been initiated or completed. Furthermore, conducting substantive review of an employee's reward application was not only a right of the employer but also an obligation. In this case, the reward established by the "Reward Measures" was a form of excess labor remuneration promised by Chengkai Company to encourage creative work by its employees. Its nature fell under the category of "other bonuses" as defined in Article 7 of the "Provisions of the National Bureau of Statistics on the Composition of Total Wages." At this point, the "Reward Measures" should not only be regarded as Chengkai Company's unilateral incentive action towards employees based on its employment autonomy but also as an agreement formed between Chengkai Company and unspecified employees, including Peng Yuxiang, regarding the acquisition of this reward.

Now that Peng Yuxiang had, through his efforts, met the conditions for obtaining the reward set by the "Reward Measures," and had submitted an application to Chengkai Company requesting the payment of this excess labor remuneration, whether based on the principle of good faith or the principle of distribution according to work, Chengkai Company had the obligation to initiate the review process to examine the reward application to determine whether Peng Yuxiang's right to the bonus could be realized. If Chengkai Company refused to review, it should provide a reasonable explanation. In this case, Chengkai Company's claims that Peng Yuxiang had committed dereliction of duty and that the projects in question had suffered losses could not be established due to lack of factual basis. The company also could not provide a reasonable explanation for its refusal to review. Its refusal to fulfill its approval obligation had harmed Peng Yuxiang's legitimate rights and interests, and it should bear the corresponding adverse consequences.

In summary, the court determined that the conditions for receiving the reward for the six projects in question had been satisfied, and Chengkai Company should, in accordance with the "Reward Measures," distribute the reward to the Investment and Development Department where Peng Yuxiang worked.

(Judges of the effective judgment: Feng Chi, Wu Xiaojing, Lu Hongxia)

Guiding Case No. 183

Fang Yue v. Sino-US United MetLife Insurance Co., Ltd. — dispute over labor contract

(Discussed and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on July 4, 2022)

Keywords: civil, labor contract, resignation, year-end bonus

Ruling Gist

If a worker who leaves before the payment of the year-end bonus claims that the employer should pay the year-end bonus, the people's court shall comprehensively consider factors such as the reason for the worker's departure, the time of departure, work performance, and degree of contribution to the employer. If the employer's internal regulations stipulate that workers who leave before the payment of the year-end bonus are not entitled to it, but the termination of the labor contract is not caused by the worker's unilateral fault or voluntary resignation, and the worker has completed the annual work tasks, and the employer cannot prove that the worker's work performance and conduct do not meet the standards for receiving the year-end bonus, the people's court shall support the claim of the worker who left before the payment of the year-end bonus for the employer to pay the year-end bonus.

【Related Laws】

Article 40 of the Labor Contract Law of the PRC

【Basic Facts】

Fang Yue worked at Sino-US United MetLife Insurance Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as MetLife Company) from January 2011. The last labor contract signed between the parties was effective from July 1, 2015 to June 30, 2017, and stipulated that Fang Yue served as Senior Manager of the Strategy Department. In October 2017, MetLife Company adjusted its organizational structure and decided to abolish the Strategy Department, resulting in the cancellation of Fang Yue's position. The parties engaged in nearly two months of negotiations regarding the modification of the labor contract, but failed to reach an agreement. On December 29, MetLife Company issued a "Notice of Termination of Labor Contract" to Fang Yue, citing significant changes in objective circumstances and the failure of the parties to reach an agreement on modifying the labor contract. Fang Yue disputed the termination decision. After going through labor arbitration procedures, he filed a lawsuit requesting reinstatement of the labor relationship with MetLife Company and also claimed double pay for the period from August to December 2017 without a signed labor contract, the year-end bonus for 2017, etc. MetLife Company's "Employee Handbook" stipulated: "Year-end bonuses are determined based on company policy, the company's performance, and employee performance, provided that the employee has been employed prior to October 1 of the current year. If an employee leaves before the month the bonus is paid or prior to that, they are not entitled to it." It was found that MetLife Company's annual year-end bonus was typically paid around March of the following year.

【Judgment】

The Shanghai Huangpu District People's Court rendered a civil judgment ( [2018] Hu 0101 Min Chu No. 10726) on October 29, 2018: 1. MetLife Company shall pay the plaintiff Fang Yue the double pay difference of RMB 192,500 for the period from August to December 2017 without a signed labor contract within seven days from the effective date of the judgment; 2. All other claims of Fang Yue are dismissed. Dissatisfied, Fang Yue appealed to the Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's Court. The Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's Court rendered a civil judgment ( [2018] Hu 02 Min Zhong No. 11292) on March 4, 2019: 1. Affirming item 1 of the civil judgment ( [2018] Hu 0101 Min Chu No. 10726) of the Shanghai Huangpu District People's Court; 2. Setting aside item 2 of the civil judgment ( [2018] Hu 0101 Min Chu No. 10726) of the Shanghai Huangpu District People's Court; 3. MetLife Company shall pay the appellant Fang Yue the pre-tax year-end bonus for 2017 of RMB 138,600 within seven days from the effective date of the judgment; 4. Other claims of Fang Yue are not supported.

法院生效裁判认为：本案的争议焦点系用人单位以客观情况发生重大变化为依据解除劳动合同，导致劳动者不符合员工手册规定的年终奖发放条件时，劳动者是否可以获得相应的年终奖。对此，一审法院认为，大都会公司的《员工手册》明确规定了奖金发放情形，房玥在大都会公司发放2017年度奖金之前已经离职，不符合奖金发放情形，故对房玥要求2017年度奖金之请求不予支持。二审法院经过审理后认为，现行法律法规并没有强制规定年终奖应如何发放，用人单位有权根据本单位的经营状况、员工的业绩表现等，自主确定奖金发放与否、发放条件及发放标准，但是用人单位制定的发放规则仍应遵循公平合理原则，对于在年终奖发放之前已经离职的劳动者可否获得年终奖，应当结合劳动者离职的原因、时间、工作表现和对单位的贡献程度等多方面因素综合考量。本案中，大都会公司对其组织架构进行调整，双方未能就劳动合同的变更达成一致，导致劳动合同被解除。房玥在大都会公司工作至2017年12月29日，此后两日系双休日，表明房玥在2017年度已在大都会公司工作满一年；在大都会公司未举证房玥的2017年度工作业绩、表现等方面不符合规定的情况下，可以认定房玥在该年度为大都会公司付出了一整年的劳动且正常履行了职责，为大都会公司做出了应有的贡献。基于上述理由，大都会公司关于房玥在年终奖发放月之前已离职而不能享有该笔奖金的主张缺乏合理性。故对房玥诉求大都会公司支付2017年度年终奖，应予支持。

（生效裁判审判人员：郭征海、谢亚琳、易苏苏）

The effective judgment of the court held that: The issue in dispute in this case is whether a worker is entitled to the corresponding year-end bonus when the employer terminates the labor contract based on a major change in objective circumstances, resulting in the worker no longer meeting the conditions for issuing the year-end bonus as stipulated in the employee handbook. In this regard, the court of first instance held that the Metropolis Company's Employee Handbook clearly specified the circumstances for issuing bonuses, and since Fang Yue had already left before the Metropolis Company issued the 2017 annual bonus, he did not meet the conditions for bonus issuance. Therefore, it did not support Fang Yue's claim for the 2017 annual bonus. After trial, the court of second instance held that the current laws and regulations do not mandate how year-end bonuses should be distributed. The employer has the right to independently decide whether to issue bonuses, as well as the conditions and standards for issuance, based on its own business conditions and the employee's performance. However, the rules formulated by the employer for issuing bonuses must still follow the principle of fairness and reasonableness. Whether a worker who has left before the issuance of the year-end bonus can obtain the bonus should be comprehensively considered based on multiple factors, including the reason for the worker's departure, the timing, work performance, and degree of contribution to the unit. In this case, the Metropolis Company adjusted its organizational structure, and the two parties failed to reach an agreement on the modification of the labor contract, leading to the termination of the labor contract. Fang Yue worked at the Metropolis Company until December 29, 2017, and the following two days were weekends, indicating that Fang Yue had worked full-time at the Metropolis Company for one year in 2017. In the absence of evidence from the Metropolis Company showing that Fang Yue's work performance and conduct in 2017 did not meet the requirements, it can be determined that Fang Yue had worked for the Metropolis Company for the entire year in 2017 and had performed his duties normally, making a due contribution to the Metropolis Company. Based on the above reasons, the Metropolis Company's argument that Fang Yue was not entitled to the bonus because he had left before the month of bonus issuance lacked reasonableness. Therefore, Fang Yue's claim requesting the Metropolis Company to pay the 2017 annual bonus should be supported.

(Judges of the effective judgment: Guo Zhenghai, Xie Yalin, Yi Susu)

Guiding Case No. 184

Ma Xiaonan v. Beijing Sohu New Power Information Technology Co., Ltd. — dispute over non-competition restriction

(Deliberated and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on July 4, 2022)

Keywords: civil / non-competition restriction / term / invalidity of agreement

Ruling Gist

If an employer and a worker stipulate in a non-competition clause that the period during which an application for arbitration or litigation is filed due to a dispute arising from the performance of the non-competition clause shall not be counted in the non-competition term, this falls under the circumstance of "the employer exempting itself from its statutory responsibilities and excluding the worker's rights" as stipulated in Article 26, paragraph 1, item (2) of the Labor Contract Law of the PRC, and shall be deemed invalid.

Related Laws

Article 23, paragraph 2; Article 24; and Article 26, paragraph 1 of the Labor Contract Law of the PRC

Basic Facts

Ma Xiaonan joined Beijing Sohu New Power Information Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Sohu New Power Company) on September 28, 2005. The term of the last labor contract between the parties was from February 1, 2014, to February 28, 2017, and Ma Xiaonan served as a Senior Director. On February 1, 2014, Sohu New Power Company (Party A) and Ma Xiaonan (Party B) signed the Non-Competition Agreement, in which Clause 3.3 stipulated: "...The non-competition term shall commence from the date of Party B's resignation, with a maximum term not exceeding 12 months. The specific number of months shall be calculated based on the non-competition compensation actually paid by Party A to Party B. However, if arbitration or litigation is initiated due to a dispute arising from the performance of this Agreement, then the above-mentioned non-competition term shall deduct the period of arbitration and litigation proceedings; that is, the term during which Party B shall perform the non-competition obligation, after deducting the period of arbitration and litigation proceedings, shall not be shorter than the agreed number of non-competition months." On February 28, 2017, the labor contract expired, and the labor relationship between the parties was terminated. On March 24, 2017, Sohu New Power Company issued to Ma Xiaonan a "Notice on Requiring Compliance with Non-Competition Obligations and Collecting Non-Competition Economic Compensation," requiring him to comply with the Non-Competition Agreement and fully and properly fulfill the non-competition obligations. After leaving Sohu New Power Company, Ma Xiaonan began cooperating with Youku Company in mid-March 2017 and later left Youku Company at the end of April 2017, thereby violating the Non-Competition Agreement. Sohu New Power Company filed an application for arbitration with the Beijing Labor and Personnel Dispute Arbitration Commission, requesting confirmation that Ma Xiaonan had violated the non-competition obligations, that he double refund the non-competition compensation, that he continue to perform the non-competition obligations, that he compensate for losses, and that he pay attorney's fees. The Arbitration Commission issued the Award Jing Lao Ren Zhong Zi [2017] No. 339, which held: (1) Ma Xiaonan shall double refund the non-competition compensation for March and April 2017 to Sohu New Power Company, totaling RMB 177,900; (2) Ma Xiaonan shall continue to perform the non-competition obligations towards Sohu New Power Company; (3) Sohu New Power Company's other arbitration requests were dismissed. Ma Xiaonan disagreed and filed a lawsuit with the Haidian District People's Court of Beijing within the statutory period.

Judgment

The Haidian District People's Court of Beijing rendered the Civil Judgment (2017) Jing 0108 Min Chu No. 45728 on March 15, 2018, holding: (1) Ma Xiaonan shall, within seven days from the effective date of the judgment, double refund the non-competition compensation for March and April 2017 to Sohu New Power Company, totaling RMB 177,892; (2) It was confirmed that Ma Xiaonan was not required to continue performing the non-competition obligations towards Sohu New Power Company. Sohu New Power Company disagreed with the first-instance judgment and appealed. The Beijing First Intermediate People's Court rendered the Civil Judgment (2018) Jing 01 Min Zhong No. 5826 on August 22, 2018, dismissing the appeal and affirming the original judgment.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held that: The issue in dispute in this case is the legal application of the non-competition term stipulated in Clause 3.3 of the Non-Competition Agreement. Sohu New Power Company argued on appeal that the stipulation in Clause 3.3 of the Agreement was valid, and that Ma Xiaonan's non-competition term should be the actual duration of the arbitration and litigation proceedings in this case plus 12 months, calculated based on the actual time and not exceeding two years. However, this court did not accept this argument.

I. Review of the Non-Competition Agreement

Although the law allows an employer to agree with a worker on non-competition obligations, it also imposes mandatory restrictions on the content of such agreements. Specifically, it explicitly restricts the scope of personnel covered, the field of competition, and the term of the non-competition obligation through mandatory norms, and requires that the non-competition agreement must not violate laws and regulations, with the aim of protecting the employer's trade secrets, maintaining the order of fair competition in the market, while also preventing the employer from improperly using the non-competition system to excessively impair the worker's right to freedom of employment.

II. Validity of the "Deduction of Arbitration and Litigation Proceedings Period" Clause

In this case, Sohu New Power Company stipulated in Clause 3.3 of the Non-Competition Agreement that Ma Xiaonan's non-competition term should deduct the period of arbitration and litigation proceedings. This stipulation effectively meant that the term during which Ma Xiaonan was required to perform the non-competition obligation was: the period of arbitration and litigation proceedings plus the number of months for which non-competition compensation was actually paid (maximum 12 months). From the perspective of the worker's right to freedom of employment, although the law sets statutory limits on the duration of arbitration and litigation proceedings, for specific cases, this period is not a fixed or definite time. Incorporating such a period as part of the non-competition term contradicts the legislative intent that non-competition clauses should be specific and definite. Additionally, given the unique nature of labor dispute cases, a considerable number of cases require one arbitration and two trials. The above stipulation would mean that once a worker becomes involved in a dispute with the employer, the non-competition term would be extended for an unforeseeable and potentially lengthy period, even up to two years. This effectively leaves the worker's right to freedom of employment in an uncertain state for a certain period. Furthermore, from the perspective of the worker's right to judicial relief, if the worker initiates arbitration and litigation due to a dispute with Sohu New Power Company over the performance of the Non-Competition Agreement, then according to the stipulation in Clause 3.3 of the Agreement, the worker would still need to perform the non-competition obligation during the arbitration and litigation proceedings, resulting in the extension of the non-competition term. This places the worker in a dilemma: "if they seek judicial relief, their non-competition term is extended; if they do not seek judicial relief, their rights are impaired," thereby to a certain extent limiting the worker's right to judicial relief. For the employer, Clause 3.3 of the Agreement allows Sohu New Power Company, without needing to negotiate with the worker, to unilaterally and indirectly extend the worker's non-competition term by initiating arbitration and litigation, thereby exempting itself from its statutory responsibilities to a certain extent. In summary, the court held that the stipulation in Clause 3.3 of the Non-Competition Agreement that the non-competition term should deduct the period of arbitration and litigation proceedings—i.e., the part stating "However, if arbitration or litigation is initiated due to a dispute arising from the performance of this Agreement... the term during which Party B shall perform the non-competition obligation, after deducting the period of arbitration and litigation proceedings, shall not be shorter than the agreed number of non-competition months"—falls under the circumstance of "the employer exempting itself from its statutory responsibilities and excluding the worker's rights" as provided in Article 26, paragraph 1, item (2) of the Labor Contract Law of the PRC, and shall be invalid. According to Article 27 of the same Law, if the invalidity of part of a labor contract does not affect the validity of the remaining parts, the remaining parts shall remain valid.

III. Determination of the Non-Competition Term in This Case

Accordingly, based on the still-valid part of Clause 3.3 of the Non-Competition Agreement, Ma Xiaonan's non-competition term should be determined based on the number of months for which Sohu New Power Company actually paid non-competition compensation to him, and shall not exceed 12 months. Given that Sohu New Power Company had already paid Ma Xiaonan non-competition compensation for a total of 12 months from March 2017 to February 2018, Ma Xiaonan's non-competition term had already expired, and he was not required to continue performing the non-competition obligations towards Sohu New Power Company.

(Judges of the effective judgment: Zhao Yue, Wang Lirui, He Rui)

Guiding Case No. 185

Yan Jialin v. Zhejiang Sheraton Resort Co., Ltd. — dispute over equal employment right

(Deliberated and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on July 4, 2022)

Keywords: civil / equal employment right / employment discrimination / regional discrimination

Ruling Gist

If an employer, when recruiting personnel, treats a worker differently without justifiable reasons based on factors such as region, gender, or other factors that have no necessary connection with the "inherent requirements of the job," this constitutes employment discrimination. If a worker claims that their equal employment right has been infringed and requests the employer to bear corresponding legal liability, the people's court shall support such a claim.

Related Laws

Article 3 and Article 26 of the Employment Promotion Law of the PRC

Basic Facts

In July 2019, Zhejiang Sheraton Resort Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Sheraton Company) published a batch of recruitment information for company personnel through the Zhilian Recruitment platform, including positions such as "Legal Specialist" and "Assistant to the Chairman of the Board." On July 3, 2019, Yan Jialin submitted job applications for the aforementioned two positions through the Zhilian Recruitment mobile app. The job resumes submitted by Yan Jialin included personal basic information such as name, gender, date of birth, registered residence location, and current city of residence, where the registered residence location was filled as "Nanyang, Henan" and the current city of residence was filled as "Xihu District, Hangzhou, Zhejiang." According to the notarial deed issued by the Hangzhou Internet Notary Public Office in Hangzhou, the notary used Yan Jialin's account and password to log into the Zhilian Recruitment app client, which showed that Yan Jialin's submitted application for the "Assistant to the Chairman of the Board" position was viewed at 14:28 on July 4, 2019, and at 28 minutes, it was given the conclusion of unsuitability, with the "reason for unsuitability: Henanese"; the application for the "Legal Specialist" position was viewed at 14:28 on the same day, and at 29 minutes, it was given the conclusion of unsuitability, with the "reason for unsuitability: Henanese." Yan Jialin incurred notary fees of RMB 1,000 for the notarial matters involved in the case. Yan Jialin filed a lawsuit with the Hangzhou Internet Court, requesting that the Sheraton Company be ordered to make an apology, pay moral damages, and bear the costs related to the litigation.

Judgment

The Hangzhou Internet Court rendered the Civil Judgment (2019) Zhe 0192 Min Chu No. 6405 on November 26, 2019, holding: (1) The defendant Sheraton Company shall, within ten days from the effective date of this judgment, compensate the plaintiff Yan Jialin for moral damages and reasonable litigation costs, totaling RMB 10,000. (2) The defendant Sheraton Company shall, within ten days from the effective date of this judgment, make an oral apology to the plaintiff Yan Jialin and publish a public apology in the Legal Daily newspaper (the content of the apology statement must be reviewed by this court); if it fails to do so within the time limit, this court will publish the main content of the judgment in a national media outlet, with the costs to be borne by the defendant Sheraton Company. (3) The plaintiff Yan Jialin's other claims were dismissed. After the judgment was pronounced, both Yan Jialin and Sheraton Company appealed. The Hangzhou Intermediate People's Court rendered the Civil Judgment (2020) Zhe 01 Min Zhong No. 736 on May 15, 2020, dismissing the appeal and affirming the original judgment.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held that: The right to equal employment is a fundamental right enjoyed by workers under the law. It has both the nature of a social right and the nature of a private right under civil law. The worker's enjoyment of the right to equal employment is a manifestation of their personal independence and freedom of will. Infringement of the right to equal employment, in the field of civil law, infringes upon the core content of the general personality right—personal dignity. An important aspect of personal dignity is the requirement of equal treatment. Employment discrimination often causes a person to feel a serious sense of insult, harming their mental or even physical health. Accordingly, a worker may file a civil lawsuit with the people's court to seek civil tort relief when their right to equal employment is infringed.

Yan Jialin submitted job applications to Sheraton Company twice, and both times were rejected by Sheraton Company on the grounds of being "unsuitable because of being from Henan." Clearly, in the recruitment process involved in this case, Sheraton Company used the geographical space criterion of the subject's origin to classify people, and based on this classification criterion, gave Yan Jialin treatment lower than what would normally be given to others, i.e., refusal to hire. It can be determined that Sheraton Company treated Yan Jialin differently based on the regional factor of being "from Henan."

Article 3 of the Employment Promotion Law of the PRC explicitly lists four types of prohibited grounds for discrimination: ethnicity, race, gender, and religious belief, and ends with the character "etc." This indicates that the provision is an open-ended, non-exhaustive list. That is, in addition to the aforementioned four grounds which are considered prohibited grounds for unreasonable differential treatment under the law, there exist other unreasonable grounds of a similar nature that are also prohibited by law. An important criterion for determining which grounds fall within the scope of "etc." in the aforementioned provision is whether the employer makes selections based on "achieved factors" closely related to the "inherent requirements of the job," such as the worker's major, education, work experience, job skills, and professional qualifications, or whether the employer makes selections based on "ascribed factors" that have no necessary connection with the "inherent requirements of the job," such as the worker's gender, registered residence, identity, region, age, appearance, ethnicity, race, and religion. The latter constitutes unreasonable employment discrimination prohibited by law. "Ascribed factors" of a worker refer to factors that people have at birth and over which they have little ability to choose or control. As a mechanism of social evaluation and adjustment, the law should not impose unequal conditions on workers based on factors over which people have little choice or control. On the contrary, it should eliminate the practical inequalities brought about by these factors. Using "ascribed factors" that have no connection whatsoever with the "inherent requirements of the job" as the standard for differential treatment in employment fundamentally violates the general principle of fairness and justice and lacks justification.

In this case, Sheraton Company treated Yan Jialin's job application differently based on the regional factor. The regional factor is an "ascribed factor" that Yan Jialin, like anyone else, cannot freely choose or control and is innate. Where Sheraton Company fails to provide objective and valid evidence to prove that the regional factor has an inevitable inherent connection with the job position applied for by Yan Jialin, or that there is another lawful purpose, the differentiation standard used by Sheraton Company is not reasonable and constitutes a prohibited ground under the law. Therefore, Sheraton Company's differential treatment of Yan Jialin based on the regional factor, which has no necessary connection with the job, in the recruitment activities involved in this case constitutes employment discrimination against Yan Jialin. It infringes upon Yan Jialin's right to equal access to job opportunities and employment treatment, and Sheraton Company was subjectively at fault. This constitutes an infringement of Yan Jialin's right to equal employment, and accordingly, Sheraton Company shall bear the civil liability of making a public apology, paying moral damages, and compensating for reasonable litigation costs.

(Judges of the effective judgment: Shi Qingrong, Yu Jianming, Kong Wenchao)
